SECTION 010:00–4:40

Keep every linear combination inside the space

A plane or line through zero can be a subspace of R³.

Lecture 6 develops two subspaces associated with a matrix: its column space and its nullspace. It begins by recalling the rule that makes a set of vectors a vector space.

Adding vectors in the set must keep the result in the set. Multiplying by any real scalar must do the same. Together, these requirements say that all linear combinations stay inside:

v, w in S   ⇒   cv + dw in S for all real c, d.

For a nonempty subset of Rⁿ with the usual operations, this is the subspace test. The algebraic rules for addition and scalar multiplication are inherited from Rⁿ.

Strang sketches a plane through the origin and a line through the origin in R³. Adding vectors within the plane stays in the plane, and any scalar multiple remains there. The same checks work for the line.

Both sets must contain the zero vector. Their drawings have finite extent on the board, but the plane and line continue indefinitely. The next questions ask what happens when we combine these two subspaces as sets.

SECTION 024:40–7:21

A union can fail the addition test

A vector from the plane plus one from the line may leave both.

The union P ∪ L contains every vector in P or in L, including vectors in both. It does not automatically include sums of vectors taken from the two different sets.

In the lecture’s picture, L is not contained in P. Choose a nonzero vector from L and a suitable vector from P. Their sum lies off the plane and off the line. It is outside their union, so addition is not closed.

For a concrete version, take P to be the plane z = 0 and L to be the vertical axis:

v = (1, 0, 0)ᵀ ∈ P,   w = (0, 0, 1)ᵀ ∈ L,
v + w = (1, 0, 1)ᵀ ∉ P ∪ L.

The sum has nonzero z, so it is outside P. It has nonzero x, so it is outside L. This one failed sum is enough to rule out a subspace.

Illustrative coordinates and scope. The vectors above give coordinates to the lecture’s geometric argument. A union does not always fail: if one subspace is contained in the other, their union is simply the larger subspace. The pictured line and plane do not have that containment.

SECTION 037:21–11:37

An intersection always remains a subspace

Vectors must satisfy both sets of requirements.

The intersection P ∩ L consists of vectors belonging to both sets. Since the pictured line crosses the plane only at the origin, their intersection is {0}. The zero vector alone is a valid subspace.

The same principle works for any two subspaces S and T of a common vector space. They both contain zero, so their intersection is nonempty.

Take v and w in S ∩ T. Both vectors lie in S, so v + w lies in S. Both also lie in T, so the same sum lies in T. Therefore it is in the intersection.

Scalar multiplication works the same way: if v is in both subspaces, then cv is in both for every real c.

v, w ∈ S ∩ T   ⇒   cv + dw ∈ S and cv + dw ∈ T
⇒ cv + dw ∈ S ∩ T.

Intersection adds requirements but preserves closure. This gives a general way to build a subspace from existing subspaces.

SECTION 0411:37–16:00

Build the column space of a four-by-three matrix

The columns have four components, so their space lies in R⁴.

The matrix used throughout the rest of the lecture is

A=[112213314415]

Call its columns a₁, a₂, and a₃. Each is in R⁴ because each contains four entries. Taking every real linear combination gives the column space:

C(A) = { x₁a₁ + x₂a₂ + x₃a₃ : x₁, x₂, x₃ ∈ R }.

The three columns by themselves do not make a subspace. Their multiples, sums, and all other combinations must be included. The column space is the smallest subspace containing them.

Adding two combinations gives another combination, and multiplying a combination by a scalar gives another one. This verifies closure.

Three vectors cannot span all of R⁴. Strang first asks this as an intuitive question, then investigates how much smaller this particular column space is. The answer will depend on relations among the columns.

SECTION 0516:00–20:15

Ask which right-hand sides can be reached

Four equations in three unknowns cannot be solved for every b.

The abstract definition of column space has a concrete purpose: understanding when a linear system has a solution. Here the system is

x₁ + x₂ + 2x₃ = b₁
2x₁ + x₂ + 3x₃ = b₂
3x₁ + x₂ + 4x₃ = b₃
4x₁ + x₂ + 5x₃ = b₄.

There are three unknowns and four equations. Each choice of x produces a vector Ax in R⁴, but those outputs do not fill all of R⁴. Consequently, arbitrary choices of b need not be possible.

Having more equations than unknowns does not make every system inconsistent. Some right-hand sides do work. The question is to identify exactly which ones.

The column picture says what an input does: its three entries are weights on the three columns. A solution is a set of weights that produces the requested b.

The question to answer

For this fixed A, which vectors b can be written as Ax for some x?

SECTION 0620:15–23:09

Find solvable examples by choosing x first

Zero and the individual columns are guaranteed right-hand sides.

The zero right-hand side always works: A0 = 0. This fact is true for every matrix, regardless of its size or dependence among its columns.

For b = a₁ = (1, 2, 3, 4)ᵀ, choose x = (1, 0, 0)ᵀ. The product takes one copy of the first column and zero copies of the others:

[112213314415][100]=[1234]

For b = a₂ = (1, 1, 1, 1)ᵀ, choose x = (0, 1, 0)ᵀ:

[112213314415][010]=[1111]

These examples avoid solving four equations from scratch. Each input selects a column. More generally, choose any x and calculate b = Ax; the resulting b is automatically one for which the system is solvable.

SECTION 0723:09–25:07

Ax = b is solvable exactly when b is in C(A)

The column space is the full set of possible outputs.

A matrix–vector product is a linear combination of the matrix’s columns. Conversely, the coefficients in any such combination form an input vector x. Therefore

Ax = b has a solution   ⇔   b ∈ C(A).

This holds for any matrix A. Its column space is exactly the set {Ax : x is an allowed input}. If b is outside that set, no choice of x can produce it.

For the present example, a₃ = a₁ + a₂. Thus every output is a combination of the first two columns alone:

b = sa₁ + ta₂ = (s + t, 2s + t, 3s + t, 4s + t)ᵀ.

The consecutive differences of these four entries are all s. Equivalently, the system is solvable precisely when

b₁ − 2b₂ + b₃ = 0,
b₂ − 2b₃ + b₄ = 0.

Conversely, if both equations hold, choose s = b₂ − b₁ and t = 2b₁ − b₂. These values reproduce the first two entries; the two conditions then force the third and fourth entries to match as well.

Explicit test added for study. The lecture states the column-space criterion and then identifies the column dependence. The parameterization and these two equations are editorial consequences for this particular A. For example, b = (1, 0, 0, 0)ᵀ fails the first equation and cannot be reached.

SECTION 0825:07–28:12

A dependent column adds no new direction

Three columns span a two-dimensional subspace of R⁴.

Does each of the three columns contribute a new direction? For this matrix, the third column is already a combination of the first two:

[1234]+[1111]=[2345]

Adding a₃ to the list of available columns creates no new combinations. Any expression involving it can be rewritten as

x₁a₁ + x₂a₂ + x₃a₃ = (x₁ + x₃)a₁ + (x₂ + x₃)a₂.

The first two columns point in genuinely different directions. If a₁ were a multiple of a₂, all entries of a₁ would be equal, but they are 1, 2, 3, and 4. So their combinations fill a two-dimensional subspace of R⁴.

Strang notes that a different column could also be discarded: a₁ = a₃ − a₂, so a₂ and a₃ generate the same space. The first-two-columns choice reflects the convention of retaining the first independent columns as pivot columns.

Count directions, not just columns

Here C(A) has dimension 2 even though A has 3 columns. Its vectors still have 4 components.

SECTION 0928:12–32:04

The nullspace contains inputs that give zero

N(A) lives in the input space, which is R³ in this example.

The second important space is the nullspace. It contains solution vectors x, rather than right-hand-side vectors b:

N(A) = { x ∈ R³ : Ax = 0 }.

The right-hand side is now fixed at the zero vector. The task is to find all inputs that produce that output.

For our four-by-three matrix, an input has three components. Therefore N(A) is a subset of R³. The column space instead lies in R⁴ because outputs and columns have four components.

For an m × n matrix A:
C(A) ⊆ Rᵐ,   N(A) ⊆ Rⁿ.

Each entry of x supplies one coefficient for a column. The number of columns is the number of input coordinates; the number of rows is the number of output coordinates.

Zero is always in N(A), since A0 = 0. This is necessary for a subspace. Later in the lecture Strang checks the remaining closure properties for every matrix.

SECTION 1032:04–36:46

Find the entire nullspace line

A relation among columns supplies a nonzero solution of Ax = 0.

The column relation immediately gives a nonzero solution:

[112213314415][11−1]=[0000]

Its entries use one copy of a₁, one of a₂, and minus one of a₃. Those columns cancel because a₃ = a₁ + a₂. Every multiple of this input also gives zero, including (2, 2, −2)ᵀ and (7, 7, −7)ᵀ.

N(A) = { (c, c, −c)ᵀ : c ∈ R }
= { c(1, 1, −1)ᵀ : c ∈ R }.

This description includes zero when c = 0 and fills an entire line in both directions through the origin.

Why these are all the solutions

The first two homogeneous equations are x₁ + x₂ + 2x₃ = 0 and 2x₁ + x₂ + 3x₃ = 0. Subtracting them gives x₁ + x₃ = 0. Substitution gives x₂ + x₃ = 0. Thus x₁ = x₂ = −x₃, exactly the form above; the remaining equations then hold automatically.

Completeness check. The lecture identifies the entire line by inspection of the columns. The two-equation calculation spells out why no other nullspace vectors are missing.

SECTION 1136:46–40:39

Prove that a nullspace is always a subspace

Linearity preserves the zero right-hand side.

The example looks like a subspace, but the name nullspace must be justified for any matrix A. Strang checks the two closure properties directly.

Take v and w with Av = 0 and Aw = 0. Matrix multiplication distributes over addition:

A(v + w) = Av + Aw = 0 + 0 = 0.

Therefore v + w is another solution of the homogeneous equations. The sum stays in N(A).

If v is a solution, any real scalar multiple is also a solution:

A(cv) = cAv = c0 = 0.

The lecture uses c = 12 as its concrete scalar example. Together with A0 = 0, these facts verify that N(A) is a subspace.

The combined statement

If Av = 0 and Aw = 0, then A(cv + dw) = 0 for every pair of real scalars c and d.

The zero right-hand side is essential. Adding two solutions with the same nonzero right-hand side instead produces twice that right-hand side. This leads to the next example.

SECTION 1240:39–44:01

A nonzero right-hand side gives a shifted line

A particular solution plus any nullspace vector stays a solution.

Change the right-hand side to b = (1, 2, 3, 4)ᵀ. We already know that xₚ = (1, 0, 0)ᵀ works, because it selects the first column.

The students find another solution, (0, −1, 1)ᵀ:

[112213314415][0−11]=[1234]

This subtracts a₂ from a₃, leaving a₁. The two solutions differ by a nullspace vector. In fact, all solutions are

x = (1, 0, 0)ᵀ + c(1, 1, −1)ᵀ
= (1 + c, c, −c)ᵀ,   c ∈ R.

Adding a nullspace vector does not change the output: A(xₚ + v) = Axₚ + Av = b + 0 = b. Conversely, if x and xₚ both solve Ax = b, then A(x − xₚ) = 0, so their difference belongs to N(A).

The solution set is a line parallel to the nullspace line, shifted to pass through xₚ. It does not pass through zero, because zero does not solve Ax = b when b is nonzero. Therefore this solution set is not a subspace.

Completed family. The lecture identifies two solutions and describes the shifted line. Its full parameterization and the particular-solution-plus-nullspace proof are editorial expansions. At c = −1, the formula gives the students’ second solution.

SECTION 1344:01–45:58

Build a space from vectors or describe it by equations

Column spaces and nullspaces express two central constructions.

The lecture ends with two ways to specify a subspace. One starts with a list of vectors and includes every linear combination. The column space is built this way from the columns of A.

The other starts with homogeneous linear equations and takes every vector satisfying them. The nullspace is described this way by Ax = 0.

C(A): all outputs Ax, generated by the columns.
N(A): all inputs x satisfying Ax = 0.

For the example, the column space is a two-dimensional subspace of R⁴ generated by a₁ and a₂. The nullspace is a one-dimensional subspace of R³ generated by (1, 1, −1)ᵀ.

Knowing the column space answers which b permit a solution. Knowing the nullspace describes the freedom among solutions: adding any nullspace vector preserves the output.

Small examples let us see these spaces by inspection. The next lecture develops systematic elimination methods for finding nullspace vectors and organizing pivot and free variables in larger systems.
